text:
Derivational Morphology is a process that derives new 
words from existing “parts.”
The “parts” (or units) are called morphemes.
The word Morphology has a pretty transparent derivation, actually:
morph- (derived from the Greek? for “form”) 
+
-ology (also from Greek, here meaning something like “the study of”)
“the study of the forms of words.”
Then a similar process gives you morpheme. We just learned about phonemes. 
“Phone” is another morpheme from the Greek (for “speech?”). 
What do we call a unit in text?
What is “graphology?”...oops.

Derivational morphology is productive, but in limited ways as we saw when we tried to 
make up new words, and guess their meanings.
The meaning of the final form is only partially predictable.
Even in the case of zero derivation, where we change the part of speech of a word, we 
are usually working with a narrow sense of the base word.
Here are the some top-ranked pictures from Google Images for “knife,” and one that 
came up for “prison shiv.”  Which of these would you use to “knife” somebody?

text:
Derivational morphology is productive, but in limited ways
...also with respect to how widely and how regularly affixes are applied.
Consider:
stem + -hood -> a state of being, associated with the stem noun
brotherhood
sisterhood
knighthood (actually kind of odd, because two brothers share their brotherhood, but 
each knight has his own knighthood..)
*neighborhood -- perfectly good word, but -hood does a different job entirely
*friendhood  -- we say friendship instead, for, like, no apparent reason
*enemyhood -- maybe ought to be a word. I can only think of top-shelf items like 
“enmity” or “antagonism” for this concept...
(some examples from Liberman & Prince’s introductory Linguistics class at Penn: 
http://www.ling.upenn.edu/courses/Fall_1998/ling001/morphology2.html Liberman also blogs at http://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu)

text:
Even zero derivation does complicated things with 
semantics.
Consider these strong associates of the noun “knife.” Are their meanings 
similar as verbs?
She can dish it out but she can’t take it.
He was born with a silver spoon and a forked tongue in his mouth.
They decided to table the issue after a day of inconclusive negotiations.
If you got really distracted by “silver spoon,” above, you may enjoy reading about Cognitive Linguistics, 
which we won’t talk about much in this class.

text:
More commonly, derivational morphology changes the 
pronunciation (and spelling) of a word, e.g., by adding 
affixes:
certificate /sər.ˈtI.fɨ.kɨt/
certification /ˌsər.tɨ.fɨ.ˈkeI.ʃən/
recertification /ˈri.sər.tɨ.fɨ.ˌkeI.ʃən/
Note how adding an affix can impact the phonology of the rest of the word. 
(This is one reason for “The Chaos” of English spelling, and why higher 
fidelity to the spoken form doesn’t necessarily improve readability. )
Also consider the noun and verb forms of:
record
invite           (“He did not receive an invite”/”We did not invite him”)
entrance      (not actually related to each other)
...where the major change is also stress.

text:
Inflectional morphology changes the meaning of words in 
a more predictable way:
PLURALS
knife(n) - knives 
one fork - two forks
one mouse - a lot of mice
3RD PERSON SINGULAR PRESENT
knife(v) - knifes 
I walk - she walks
you run - he runs
PAST
knife(v) - knifed
Today I walk - yesterday I walked
Today she sings - in the past, she sang
Menn puts this succinctly:
“...we’d think it was silly to have 
separate dictionary entries for the 
singular and plural forms of 
nouns.”
But note that the phonological 
process of inflecting words often 
has some irregularity to it. 
(This will be a big deal later when 
we talk about different language 
learning models, and kinds of 
developmental language 
impairment.)

text:
Inflectional morphology also depends on the syntax of 
the rest of the sentence.
In the phrase 
“two [noun]+pl” 
whatever noun goes there must be pluralized somehow. 
There are no syntactic processes like this for even very 
productive derivational forms. 
The closest I can think of is a formula, like:
“Once you [verb] it, you can un-[verb] it.” 
But that’s not syntax.
PLURALS
knife(n) - knives 
one fork - two forks
...etc.

text:
An aside: English is pretty limited in its use of inflection
PLURALS
knife(n) - knives
one fork - two forks
one mouse - a lot of mice
3RD PERSON SINGULAR (PRESENT)
knife(v) - knifes
I walk - she walks
you run - he runs
PAST
knife(v) - knifed
Today I walk - yesterday I walked
Today she sings - in the past, she sang
...and tense! 
Further, many languages also have case
markings for nouns, which encode 
information about syntactic/semantic 
roles. 
Many languages have different 
ways of forming the plural for small 
and large numbers.
Many languages conjugate verbs 
much more elaborately than 
English for person...

text:
Summary so far:
Both inflectional and derivational morphology:
create new (phonological) forms out of old parts 
change the meanings of base forms
Derivational morphology:
creates new words
is productive, but not always, and typically limited
Inflectional morphology:
changes how words interact (syntactically) with other words
is highly productive, but not always regular
is required by syntax

More than words...
Phrases,

dealt with single words (verbs and nouns).
Those are kinds of content words. Other content word classes include modifiers like 
adjectives and adverbs. 
We haven’t dealt with function words yet, because we haven’t tried putting more than 
a couple of words together. So, now consider the noun phrases between {curly brackets} 
below:

text:
Without some way of abstracting away from the details (individual words in this case), 
we have no way of talking about these very different surface forms as similar.
Further, it would be impossible to talk about similarities and differences between 
languages coherently without this level of abstraction  All languages have NPs, but they 
can form them very differently. Here’s one in Chinese that goes PP + N
咖啡店裡面的小貓 
coffeeshop inside + cat
(the cat in the coffee shop)
Note the lack of a determiner in the Chinese NP.  This helps explain why learning to use 
determiners is so difficult for speakers of Chinese languages to learn determiners in L2.
Why do we need this level of abstraction?

Prepositional Phrases
The video for “More than Words”
We just saw a ton of prepositional phrases. 
Breaking them down will reveal a their general structure:
from + { the + early  + ‘nineties }
P     +              { NP }      (NP:  Det + Adj. + N )
with + {only one + hit}
P      + {NP}     (NP: P +  Det + N)     
{unrelated to} + {early + ‘nineties + one-hit + wonder + Extreme}
{P}   + {NP}       (NP: Adv + Adj + Adv + Adj + N)
So, all these prepositional phrases are just P + NP!

text:
More clauses
A simple, one-clause sentence:
{The plums + that were in the icebox} {were delicious}.
{Det. + N + PP}  {VP}
This is what we mean by “controls:” the verb agrees with “plums,” not “icebox”, 
because “plums” is the head of the noun phrase.
The plums in the icebox, which you were probably saving for breakfast, were delicious.
Now we have a sentence that’s a clause within a clause, set off with commas: 
“you” is the subject of “were probably saving for breakfast”, and “plums” is the 
subject of “were delicious.”
Which verb would change if we changed “you” to “my roommate?”
Forgive me.
(The subject of the first clause is implicit. The speaker wants whoever shares his 
icebox to forgive him for eating the plums.)

Syntactic and Semantic roles
These two sentences mean the same thing, but syntactically they’re 
very different:
I have eaten {the plums in the icebox}.
The plums in the icebox were eaten {by me}.
In the first case, the subject (I) appears first, followed by a verb 
phrase.
The verb phrase includes the bracketed NP, which is the object. of 
the verb. 
In the second case, “the plums in the icebox” becomes the subject. 
We can tell because the verb “were eaten,” agrees with the plural 
noun. 
Here, “by me” is just a PP fleshing out the VP.

text:
Syntactic and Semantic roles
The plums in the icebox were eaten {by me}.
If the idea that “me” is not the subject here seems counterintuitive, it’s because the way we 
usually speak in English aligns the syntactic subject of a sentence with its agent.
(In grade school, we’re taught that grammar tells us “who did what to whom.” This job is done by 
semantic roles, more so than syntactic ones.)
We have:
{The plums} {in the icebox} were eaten {by me}
{Undergoer} + {Location} + Verb + {Agent}
Alternatively:
I + have eaten {the plums} {in the icebox}.
Agent + Verb + Undergoer + Location
So, the semantic roles don’t change.
How different relationships between syntactic and semantic roles influence processing is 
something we’ll discuss more when we talk about sentence processing.

text:
Summary
Language is highly generative:
- We can make new words (derivational morphology)
- We can organize words into clauses, clauses into phrases, and phrases 
into sentences (syntax)
- We modify words for different syntactic roles (inflectional 
morphology)
We do this mostly without thinking explicitly about it.
One of the hardest things to understand about Linguistics is what there 
is to explain, because some of the most complex phenomena are 
hiding in plain sight.
